docs.text: Baseline. The steady-state checks must pass before anything is injected. If the target is not healthy to begin with, the run ends as refused and no chaos happens. A failure you cannot attribute to the experiment proves nothing. Chaos. The faults are rolled every interval_seconds (the first roll is immediate) until duration_seconds pass or max_injections injections have started. Everything the agent already guarantees applies: the kill switch, one injection per type at a time, the resource budget, cleanup on abort. Recovery. Injections still running are left to finish (everything that can stop a run, such as an abort, the kill switch, a closing window or a removed label, stays active until they have). Then the steady state is checked for up to recovery_timeout_seconds . Verdict. Verdict Meaning confirmed The steady state was restored after the chaos. falsified The steady state was not restored within recovery_timeout_seconds , or the run was aborted because an SLO was breached. Worth investigating. inconclusive The run was cut short by something other than the system (operator abort, kill switch, shutdown, a closing window, a removed label), was refused, hit an error, or an SLO could not be checked. Nothing can be concluded. GET /experiment-runs/{id} shows the status ( checking_baseline , running , recovering , completed , aborted , refused , error ), the verdict, the reason for anything other than a clean result, and the last steady-state round before and after the chaos with each check's outcome and latency. The steady state ( steady_state ) is checked before and after the chaos. To check the system while the chaos runs, and stop early if it leaves its limits, add an slo block.

A boundary inside the skipped or repeated hour resolves the way Python's zoneinfo does.
docs.title: Time windows

docs.text: A blackout is a date range when the experiment must never run, whatever the windows say: a deploy freeze, a sale, a holiday. windows : timezone : Pacific/Honolulu allow : - days : [ mon , tue , wed , thu ] start : "10:00" end : "16:00" blackouts : - from : 2026-12-20 to : 2027-01-03 reason : holiday freeze Field Notes from , to Dates, YYYY-MM-DD , both inclusive , whole days in timezone . to must not be before from ; a blackout lasts at most 366 days. Quoted or not (YAML turns bare dates into dates, which is fine). reason Optional, up to 100 characters. Shown in refusals and in the API. A blackout beats an allowed window. A window that falls inside one is closed. A window that would run into a blackout is cut off at its start: the fit check and the mid-run abort both use that, so chaos stops when the freeze begins. Overlapping or touching blackouts count as one and keep both reasons. allow can be left out: "any time except these dates". The next opening skips over blackouts, and lands on a real window, not just on the day after the blackout ends. What the agent does with them: When What happens You start a run in a blackout Refused with 409 : In a blackout period (holiday freeze); the next allowed time opens ... . You start a run outside every window Refused with 409 . The message gives the next opening in the window's own zone. No run is created and nothing is probed. You start a run but the chaos would outlast the window Refused with 409 . The estimate is the schedule plus the longest single fault (with max_injections , the time until the last allowed injection starts, plus the longest fault). The baseline and recovery checks are not counted. The window closes during the baseline check The run ends refused . Nothing was injected. The window closes during the chaos The run is aborted, injections are cut short and their effects removed. Verdict inconclusive , reason "the allowed time window closed". Dry run Never blocked. It runs, and its selection says what a real run would have been told. There is no override in the API. A window is a safety limit; to change it, edit the config and POST /config/reload . The windows decide only whether a run may happen. Nothing starts an experiment on its own, so a window never triggers one. GET /experiments and GET /experiments/{name} show whether each window is open now and when it closes or next opens (UTC), and a run reports window_closes_at .
docs.title: Blackouts

docs.text: Endpoint Role GET /experiments viewer Summaries of every defined experiment. GET /experiments/{name} viewer One experiment in full, with whether its window is open and whether this agent matches its selector. GET /experiments/{name}/selection viewer Every selection gate with its reason; whether this agent would run it now. GET /target viewer The labels this agent has, which selectors are matched against. POST /experiments/{name}/run operator Start a run. Returns 202 and the run. Optional body {"dry_run": true} . GET /experiment-runs viewer Recent runs, newest first (the last 50 are kept in memory). GET /experiment-runs/{id} viewer One run. POST /experiment-runs/abort operator End the running experiment now. Experiments cannot be created or edited through the API. A remote caller can only run what the operator defined in the config file, so the steady-state URLs and fault parameters stay under operator control. POST /config/reload picks up changes for the next run; a run in progress keeps the copy it started with.
docs.title: API

docs.text: POST /experiments/{name}/run returns: Status When 404 No such experiment. 409 The agent loop is running; another experiment is running; an injection is running; the kill switch is holding chaos back; this agent does not match the experiment's selector ; or the experiment is outside its time windows (or would not finish before one closes). 422 A fault does not fit the container's resource budget (same rule as a manual injection), or the body is invalid. 503 The agent is shutting down. Dry runs are not refused for the injection, kill switch, budget, selector, sample, eligibility or time window reasons, since they change nothing. They run, and the run records which of those a real run would have hit (see Why was this agent (not) selected? ). While an experiment runs, POST /agent/start and non-dry-run POST /inject/manual return 409 . Two sources of chaos at once would make the result unreadable.
docs.title: Refusals

docs.text: The kill switch gates experiments like everything else. If it trips mid-run, the injections are aborted and the run ends aborted with an inconclusive verdict. Stop an experiment with POST /experiment-runs/abort , not POST /agent/stop (that one only stops the agent loop). POST /inject/abort cuts running injections short, but the experiment keeps rolling its schedule. A closing time window, or labels that stop matching the selector, abort a running experiment the same way. Shutdown aborts a running experiment and removes its effects before exiting. Every start and finish is in the audit log ( experiment.started , experiment.finished ). The injections inside a run are recorded with source: experiment , the experiment name and the run id, attributed to the person who started it.
docs.title: Safety

docs.text: The steady state tells you whether the system came back. An SLO is a limit it must stay within while the chaos runs , and the experiment stops the moment it does not. Without one, an experiment injects for its full schedule whatever happens to your users. experiments : - name : cpu-recovery # ... slo : checks : - type : prometheus name : error-rate url : http://prometheus.monitoring:9090 query : > sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m])) operator : "<" threshold : 0.01 - type : prometheus name : p99-latency url : http://prometheus.monitoring:9090 query : > histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le)) operator : "<" threshold : 0.5 check_interval_seconds : 5 breach_after : 2 grace_seconds : 60 Field Default Range Notes checks required 1 to 10 http or prometheus checks, names unique. All must pass in a round. check_interval_seconds 5 1 to 60 Time between rounds. breach_after 2 1 to 20 Failing rounds in a row before it trips. A passing round resets the count, so one noisy sample does not end an experiment. grace_seconds 0 0 to 600 Wait this long after the chaos starts before the first round. For metrics that need time to show an effect, such as a rate(...[1m]) window.
docs.title: SLO abort

docs.text: Situation Result A check evaluated and violated its limit The run is aborted: injections are cut short and their effects removed. Status aborted , verdict falsified , reason SLO breached: error-rate: 0.08 is not < 0.01 . The system did not stay within its limits, which is what the experiment exists to find. A check could not be evaluated (metrics server down, query rejected, no data) Aborted too, verdict inconclusive , reason SLO could not be checked: ... . Nothing can be concluded about the system, but carrying on without being able to see it is not safe. Both kinds in one round A violated limit wins: falsified. It is watched for the whole chaos phase, including while the last injections finish after the schedule ends. After an SLO abort the chaos is already gone, so the agent still waits up to recovery_timeout_seconds for the steady state to return and records whether it did. The run's slo field shows the rounds so far, the last round's results, and whether and how it tripped. It is live while the run is in progress. Dry runs evaluate the SLO checks and record the result, but are never aborted by them. A dry run is therefore also the way to prove your queries are right and Prometheus is reachable before a real run.
docs.title: What happens on a breach

docs.text: - type : prometheus name : error-rate url : http://prometheus.monitoring:9090 query : 'sum(rate(errors_total[1m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[1m]))' operator : "<" threshold : 0.01 timeout_seconds : 5 on_no_data : fail bearer_token_env : PROM_TOKEN Field Default Notes url required The Prometheus base URL ( /api/v1/query is added). http or https , no credentials in the URL. query required A PromQL instant query, up to 1000 characters. It must return one value: aggregate with sum() , avg() , max() or histogram_quantile() . operator , threshold required The check passes while value <operator> threshold ( < , <= , > , >= ). timeout_seconds 5 1 to 30. on_no_data fail When the query returns nothing (or NaN, as 0/0 does with no traffic): fail counts it as unavailable , pass counts it as passing. bearer_token_env none The name of an environment variable holding a bearer token. The token itself never goes in the config. A query that cannot be answered is unavailable , not a breach: the server is down or slow, it returned an HTTP error or a malformed or oversized response (over 1 MiB), the query was rejected, it returned several series, or the token variable is not set. Redirects are not followed. Only the status code or error type is recorded, never a server message or the token. The query runs on a Prometheus you chose in the config, and the API cannot create or change experiments, so a caller can only run queries you wrote.

docs.text: Kill Switch ¶ The kill switch pauses chaos automatically when your application becomes unhealthy, and lets it resume once the application has recovered. It exists so that an experiment that goes wrong stops itself instead of waiting for a person. It protects the agent loop, the standalone agent, and POST /inject/manual . How it works ¶ It watches your application's health endpoint and acts like a circuit breaker: State Chaos What happens closed Allowed Health is checked every health_check_interval_seconds . consecutive_failures_threshold failures in a row trip it. open Paused In-flight injections are aborted and their effects removed. After recovery_test_interval_seconds it moves to half-open. half-open Paused recovery_success_threshold healthy checks in a row close it. One failed check re-opens it at once. Chaos is paused, not stopped . The agent loop keeps running, skips injections while the breaker is not closed, and carries on by itself after recovery. GET /status shows paused_by_kill_switch . It only watches while chaos is active ¶ The kill switch checks health only while chaos is armed: the loop is running, or an injection is in flight. While idle it counts nothing, so an application that is down for its own reasons does not trip it. (If it is already tripped, it keeps checking so it can detect recovery.) Grace periods ¶ After a process kill ( grace_after_process_kill_seconds ): killing the target takes it down on purpose, so health checks are skipped for a while. Manual process kills earn this grace too. After chaos becomes active ( grace_after_agent_start_seconds ): a target that is still starting up does not trip it. It applies each time chaos is armed. What counts as healthy ¶ Any 2xx response. A timeout, a connection error, any other status code, or an error inside the check itself counts as a failure. The check fails closed: a bug in the safety mechanism trips it rather than silently leaving chaos unprotected. Configuration ¶ kill_switch : enabled : true target_health_url : "http://localhost:8080/health" health_check_interval_seconds : 10 health_check_timeout_seconds : 2 # must not exceed the interval consecutive_failures_threshold : 3 grace_after_process_kill_seconds : 60 grace_after_agent_start_seconds : 30 recovery_test_interval_seconds : 120 recovery_success_threshold : 3 resume_after_recovery : true allow_api_disable : false Set target_health_url to your application's real health endpoint. In Kubernetes the sidecar shares the pod network, so localhost and your app's port work. Setting Range Notes health_check_interval_seconds 1 to 3600 health_check_timeout_seconds 1 to 60 Must not exceed the interval consecutive_failures_threshold 1 to 100 Time to trip is about interval x threshold grace_after_process_kill_seconds 0 to 3600 grace_after_agent_start_seconds 0 to 3600 recovery_test_interval_seconds 1 to 3600 recovery_success_threshold 1 to 100 target_health_url http or https , no credentials, up to 2048 characters These settings can only be changed in the config file. The API rejects any attempt to change them, so a remote caller cannot weaken the protection. Resume or latch ¶ resume_after_recovery: true (default): chaos resumes by itself after recovery. resume_after_recovery: false : after a trip, chaos stays off even once the target has recovered, until an operator calls POST /kill-switch/reset . A standalone agent has no API, so it must be restarted. Use this when an unattended restart of chaos after a failure is not acceptable. API ¶ Endpoint Purpose GET /kill-switch/status State, last health check and result, trip count and reason, time until the next recovery test POST /kill-switch/reset Close the breaker and clear any latch. The target must pass a health check right now ; otherwise it returns 409. POST /inject/manual Returns 409 Chaos paused: ... while the breaker is not closed. Dry runs are always allowed. POST /agent/start Starts the loop. enable_kill_switch=false is refused (403) unless allow_api_disable: true . One kill switch lives for the whole process. Stopping and starting the agent, or reloading the config, does not clear a trip. Reloading applies new settings but keeps the current state. Only recovery or a verified reset closes it. Metrics ¶ Metric Meaning chaos_kill_switch_state 0 closed, 1 open, 2 half-open chaos_kill_switch_trips_total Number of trips chaos_kill_switch_health_checks_total{result} Health checks made, healthy or unhealthy Alert on chaos_kill_switch_state != 0 . Disabling it ¶ Set kill_switch.enabled: false . The agent logs a warning at startup and chaos runs without automatic protection. Only do this if something else is watching. To let operators bypass it for a single run through the API, set allow_api_disable: true ; then POST /agent/start?enable_kill_switch=false skips it for that run only. The default is that nobody can. Known gaps ¶ One health endpoint, one signal. It does not look at error rates or latency from Prometheus. That belongs with the experiment model in the roadmap. A short manual injection can finish inside the grace period , before any health check runs. The gate still stops new injections once tripped. Latched state is not persisted. Restarting the process starts closed. Detection takes time : about interval x threshold seconds, so keep injections short relative to that, or lower the interval.

docs.text: Kubernetes Deployment ¶ The agent runs as a sidecar in the same pod as your application. k8s/chaos-demo.yaml is a complete working example. This page covers deploying it and what to carry over to your own workloads. Deploy the Demo ¶ You need a cluster (kind, minikube or cloud) with the two images loaded. See Installation . kubectl apply -f k8s/chaos-demo.yaml kubectl -n chaos-demo create secret generic chaos-api-token \ --from-literal = token = " $( openssl rand -hex 32 ) " \ --from-literal = metrics-token = " $( openssl rand -hex 32 ) " kubectl -n chaos-demo logs -l app = resilient-app -c chaos-agent -f The pod stays in ContainerCreating until the Secret exists. The demo config sets agent.auto_start: true , so chaos begins on its own. What the Manifest Creates ¶ Resource Purpose Namespace chaos-demo Keeps the demo isolated ConfigMap chaos-config The agent's config.yaml Deployment resilient-app One pod with the target-app and chaos-agent containers Service resilient-app The target app on port 8080 Service chaos-agent-api Metrics on port 8000. The control API is deliberately not exposed NetworkPolicies Deny everything, then allow the app within the namespace, metrics from a monitoring namespace, and DNS Reach the Agent ¶ # Control API kubectl -n chaos-demo port-forward deploy/resilient-app 9000 :9000 TOKEN = $( kubectl -n chaos-demo get secret chaos-api-token -o jsonpath = '{.data.token}' | base64 -d ) curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN " http://127.0.0.1:9000/status Prometheus scrapes chaos-agent-api.chaos-demo:8000 with the metrics token. See Monitoring . To rotate a token, update the Secret; see API Security . Adapt It for Your Workload ¶ Your pod spec needs the following, all of which the demo has: shareProcessNamespace: true , so the agent can see and signal the app's processes. Capabilities NET_ADMIN and KILL , with everything else dropped. NET_ADMIN is for network latency ( tc ), KILL for signalling the app. Resource limits on the chaos-agent container. CPU and memory injections are sized to a fraction of them, so they are the blast-radius boundary. With safety.require_cgroup_limits: true the agent refuses to inject if the limits are missing. The token Secret , mounted and referenced by CHAOS_API_TOKEN_FILE and CHAOS_METRICS_TOKEN_FILE . Pod labels from the downward API ( CHAOS_TARGET_LABELS_FILE ), if you use experiment selectors or eligibility. Point kill_switch.target_health_url at your app's health endpoint. The sidecar shares the pod network, so localhost reaches it. Change the Configuration ¶ The ConfigMap is mounted with subPath , so edits do not reach a running pod. After editing it, restart: kubectl -n chaos-demo rollout restart deployment/resilient-app Clean Up ¶ kubectl delete namespace chaos-demo For AWS EKS with Terraform, see Terraform (AWS EKS) .

docs.text: Process Targeting ¶ How the process failure decides which process to kill, and what it will never kill. Short version ¶ target_name is matched exactly (case-insensitive) against the process's names. It is never a substring, and it never looks at command-line arguments. It kills one process, chosen the same way every time. It will never kill the agent, anything above or below the agent, critical system processes, or PID 1. It reports success only if the process is actually gone. What target_name matches ¶ A process matches if target_name equals any of these (ignoring case): Source Example process Matches The process name nginx nginx The executable file name /opt/bin/billing billing argv[0] 's file name /usr/bin/myapp --port 80 myapp The script, module or jar of an interpreter python -u target-app.py target-app or target-app.py python -m src.api_server src.api_server or api_server java -jar /opt/Billing.jar billing or billing.jar Interpreters recognised for the last row: python , pypy , java , node , nodejs , deno , bun , ruby , perl , php , and the common shells. Examples with target_name: "target-app" : Process Match? Why python target-app.py Yes script name target-app Yes process name tail -f /var/log/target-app.log No only an argument mentions it kubectl logs target-app No argument target-app-helper No a longer name, not equal vim target-app.py No vim is not an interpreter Linux cuts a process's kernel name to 15 characters. A longer target_name is also compared against that truncated form. To see what the agent sees, run ps -eo pid,comm,args inside the agent container and use the comm , the executable, or the script name. A dry run ( POST /inject/manual with "dry_run": true ) logs the candidates and the choice. What is never killed ¶ The agent itself, its parent, and every ancestor and descendant. Zombies, and kernel threads (processes with no command line). Critical system processes : systemd, init, tini, dockerd, containerd, runc, kubelet and other kube-* components, sshd, NetworkManager, the Kubernetes pause process, and similar. PID 1 of the PID namespace the agent shares (see below). How the critical list is matched ¶ Against the process's executable names only (name, executable, argv[0] ), and only as a whole word , where a word is bounded by anything that is not a letter or digit. Executable Protected? systemd-journald , containerd-shim-runc-v2 , dumb-init Yes (the critical name is a whole word) initialize , truncate-job , reinit , paused No (they only contain init , runc , pause ) python initialize.py No (only the executable counts, not the script argument) pause-service , init-db Yes. A hyphen-separated word counts. Rename the executable if you need to target it Earlier versions matched the whole command line as a substring, so python initialize.py and truncate-job were wrongly treated as critical. Choosing one process ¶ When several processes match, exactly one is killed, and the choice never depends on the order the operating system lists processes: target_selection Picks oldest (default) The process that started first (ties break on the lower PID). Usually the parent or master. newest The process that started last. Usually the latest worker. All candidates and the chosen PID are logged at INFO ( Several processes match; choosing one ). To target one specific process, use target_pid . With both set, the process must match both, which protects against PID reuse: curl -s -H " $H " -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -X POST localhost:9000/inject/manual \ -d '{"failure_type":"process","config":{"target_pid":4242}}' target_pid must be 2 or higher. PIDs change between runs, so it is mainly for manual injections. Termination ¶ Send SIGTERM and wait up to 3 seconds. If it is still running, send SIGKILL and wait up to 2 seconds. Count the injection as success only if the process is gone. A process that survives SIGKILL, an access-denied error, or a refusal is counted as failed with the reason logged. PID 1 and Docker Compose ¶ In Kubernetes ( shareProcessNamespace: true ) the pod's pause process is PID 1, your app is PID 2 or higher, and everything works. In Docker Compose the agent joins the target container's PID namespace ( pid: "service:target-app" ). If the target is the container's main process, it is PID 1 , and two kernel rules make it impossible to kill from the agent: A signal sent to PID 1 from inside its own PID namespace is discarded unless PID 1 has a handler for it. SIGKILL is always discarded. kill still reports success, so the old code logged a successful kill that never happened. If PID 1 did exit, the kernel would kill every process in the namespace , including the agent. So the agent refuses ( Refusing to kill PID 1 of the shared PID namespace ), counts it as failed , and sends nothing. A dry run shows would_be_refused: true . Fix: run the target under an init so the application is not PID 1. The Compose file in this repo sets init: true on target-app , which puts tini at PID 1 and the application at PID 2. Even then, when the application dies, tini exits and the container with it. The kernel tears down the namespace and the agent goes with it. The Compose file sets restart: always on the agent so it comes back with the restarted target. In Kubernetes this does not happen, because pause stays up when your app dies. Troubleshooting ¶ Symptom Cause and fix No killable processes found matching target The name did not match exactly. Check ps -eo pid,comm,args in the agent container and use the comm , executable or script name. A substring or an argument no longer matches. Worked before, finds nothing now You relied on substring or argument matching. Use the exact name. Refusing to kill PID 1 The target is PID 1 of the shared namespace. Run it under an init ( init: true in Compose) or use Kubernetes. Invalid target name Too short, a generic name such as python , or an unsafe character. The process you expected is not chosen Several match. Check the Several processes match log, then set target_selection or target_pid . A target named like pause-service is never found Its executable contains a critical name as a whole word. Rename it.

docs.text: Shutdown and Cleanup ¶ What happens to an injection's effect when something stops it, and the one case that no code can fully cover. Guarantees by scenario ¶ What happens Result SIGTERM or SIGINT (standalone agent or API server) In-flight injections are woken and aborted, the tc rule is removed, CPU workers are stopped, and the process exits promptly. It does not wait out the injection. POST /agent/stop The loop stops and any running injection is aborted. Its effect is removed within milliseconds, not at the end of its duration. POST /inject/abort Aborts every running injection (manual or from the loop). The loop keeps running. Kill switch trips Running injections are aborted and their effects removed. The loop keeps running but pauses chaos until the target recovers. Normal interpreter exit or an unhandled exception Cleanups run from an atexit hook. SIGKILL , OOM kill, node failure No code can run. See After a hard kill . The API server needed special handling. uvicorn's graceful shutdown waits for running background tasks, and an injection can last 5 minutes. Without a signal hook, SIGTERM during an injection would wait it out, and Kubernetes would SIGKILL the pod after its grace period with the rule still applied. The server now cleans up the moment the signal arrives, before uvicorn begins its own shutdown. After a hard kill ¶ If the agent is killed without warning while a network rule is applied, the rule stays in the pod's network namespace. In Kubernetes that namespace belongs to the pod, so a restarted container inherits it, and your target keeps its added latency. To repair this, the agent checks at startup whether the interface in its network config still has a netem rule, and removes it (it logs Removed stale network rule left by a previous run ). This runs whether or not the network failure is currently enabled. What this means in practice: Until the agent starts again, the latency remains. If the container never restarts, remove it yourself: kubectl -n chaos-demo exec deploy/resilient-app -c chaos-agent -- tc qdisc del dev eth0 root Deleting the pod always clears it, because the network namespace goes with it. The agent treats a netem root qdisc on the configured interface as its own. It never removes other kinds of root qdisc during cleanup or repair. CPU workers are the other process-level leftover. They are daemons and check once every 0.2 seconds that their parent is alive, so a killed agent does not leave workers burning CPU until their duration runs out. Memory is returned by the kernel when the process dies. One injection per type ¶ Only one injection of each type ( cpu , memory , network ) runs at a time. Overlapping ones used to be able to corrupt each other's cleanup. The agent loop leaves a type alone while its previous injection is still running (a debug log line, no warning, not counted). This is the normal case when duration_seconds is longer than interval_seconds . Any other request that arrives while one is running is skipped : logged with the reason and counted as chaos_injections_total{status="skipped"} . Injections of different types may run at the same time. The loop starts each on its own thread and does not wait for it, so a long CPU burn no longer delays a network or process injection. They share one resource budget (see blast radius ). POST /inject/manual returns 409 ( A network injection is already running ), or 503 while the agent is shutting down. Dry runs are never blocked. Process kills are instantaneous and are not guarded. GET /status lists what is running under active_injections . Every tc command and every change to rule ownership happens under one lock, and a rule is removed only by the injection that applied it (or by shutdown). A late cleanup from an old injection can therefore never delete a rule that a newer one applied. Known gaps ¶ Latency persists after a hard kill until the next agent start (above). The managed interface's root qdisc is replaced during an injection. If something else (a CNI bandwidth plugin, for example) had a root qdisc on that interface, it is removed when the injection starts and is not restored when it ends. This predates this change. Aborted injections still count as success in the metrics, since the effect was applied. --reload (development only) uses uvicorn's reloader, which bypasses the signal hook. The lifespan and atexit cleanups still run. Verifying it yourself ¶ With Docker (needs the netem kernel module on the host): export CHAOS_API_TOKEN = $( openssl rand -hex 32 ) docker run -d --name chaos --cap-add NET_ADMIN --cap-add KILL \ -p 127 .0.0.1:9000:9000 -e CHAOS_API_TOKEN -e CHAOS_API_HOST = 0 .0.0.0 \ -v $PWD /config.yaml:/app/config.yaml:ro py-chaos-agent:1.0.0 # start a 5 minute network injection, then confirm the rule exists curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CHAOS_API_TOKEN " -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -X POST localhost:9000/inject/manual \ -d '{"failure_type":"network","config":{"duration_seconds":300}}' docker exec chaos tc qdisc show dev eth0 # shows a netem rule # SIGTERM mid-injection: the container should stop within a second or two docker stop chaos Then repeat with docker kill chaos (SIGKILL) and docker start chaos , and check the log for Removed stale network rule left by a previous run .

docs.text: Terraform (AWS EKS) ¶ terraform/ builds a demo EKS cluster, a VPC and two ECR repositories. Remote state ¶ State lives in S3 with native locking (Terraform 1.10 or newer), not on your laptop. The bucket is yours, so terraform/backend.tf only declares the backend and you supply the details. Create the bucket once, with versioning, encryption and no public access: BUCKET = my-org-terraform-state REGION = us-east-1 aws s3api create-bucket --bucket " $BUCKET " --region " $REGION " # Outside us-east-1, add: --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$REGION" aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket " $BUCKET " \ --versioning-configuration Status = Enabled aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket " $BUCKET " \ --server-side-encryption-configuration \ '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"}}]}' aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket " $BUCKET " \ --public-access-block-configuration \ BlockPublicAcls = true,IgnorePublicAcls = true,BlockPublicPolicy = true,RestrictPublicBuckets = true Then point Terraform at it: cd terraform cp backend.hcl.example backend.hcl # set your bucket name; backend.hcl is git-ignored terraform init -backend-config = backend.hcl Already have local state? Add -migrate-state to the init command and answer yes . Commit .terraform.lock.hcl after the first init . It pins the provider versions and checksums. The Kubernetes API endpoint ¶ By default the cluster API is reachable from the internet, protected by IAM. That keeps the demo easy to start, and Terraform prints a warning on every plan about it. Tighten it: # Only your own address terraform apply -var 'cluster_endpoint_public_access_cidrs=["203.0.113.7/32"]' # Private cluster: no public endpoint at all terraform apply -var cluster_endpoint_public_access = false With a private endpoint, kubectl only works from inside the VPC (a VPN, a bastion host or SSM). The nodes always use the private endpoint. Variable Default Purpose cluster_endpoint_private_access true API reachable inside the VPC. Keep it on. cluster_endpoint_public_access true API reachable from the internet. cluster_endpoint_public_access_cidrs ["0.0.0.0/0"] Who may reach the public endpoint. Container registry ¶ Both ECR repositories scan images on push, encrypt them, and use immutable tags : a tag that has been pushed can never be overwritten. Push a new version for every build, matching the tag in k8s/chaos-demo.yaml : REPO = $( terraform output -json ecr_repo_urls | jq -r .chaos_agent ) aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin " ${ REPO %%/* } " docker tag py-chaos-agent:1.0.0 " $REPO :1.0.0" docker push " $REPO :1.0.0" Pushing :latest twice now fails. Untagged images are removed after 7 days, and only the newest 30 images per repository are kept.

Dry-run mode enabled: # Check config agent : dry_run : true # This prevents actual chaos! # Fix: Set to false agent : dry_run : false 2.
